summary: The article challenges outdated nutrition myths about fueling young athletes, covering carbo-loading, protein powders, dietary fat, hydration, and meal timing. It cites Dr. Samantha Pearson and coach Michael Thompson, favoring whole foods, complex carbs, unsaturated fats, and water over supplements. It concludes that nutrition should be individualized and that kids should be educated to make smart choices themselves.
one_line: Debunks youth sports nutrition myths on carbs, protein powder, fat, hydration and timing, urging whole foods, individualized plans, and education of young athletes.
key_facts: Carbo-loading, such as serving heaps of pasta the night before a big match, is an outdated approach; carb quality and timing matter more.
Dr. Samantha Pearson, a pediatric sports nutritionist, says "Not all carbs are created equal."
Complex carbohydrates from whole grains, fruits, and vegetables release energy steadily, unlike refined carbs, which cause a spike and slump.
The article suggests brown rice, quinoa, or sweet potatoes served throughout the day before an event instead of white spaghetti.
The American Academy of Pediatrics advises that most children, including athletes, get enough protein from their regular diet.
Local sports coach Michael Thompson says "Real food offers so much more than just protein" and questions athletes chugging protein shakes after every practice.
Grilled chicken breast, fish, or legume-packed chili provide protein along with vitamins and other nutrients.
Unsaturated fats from nuts, seeds, fish, and plant oils reduce inflammation, give long-lasting energy, and support brain health.
Dehydration can decrease coordination and cognitive function; athletes should hydrate before, during, and after activity.
Electrolyte drinks can help during intense exercise, especially in heat, but water should always be the first choice.
A small, carbohydrate-rich meal about two hours before game time provides energy without digestive discomfort.
After a game, athletes should eat a mix of protein to rebuild muscles and carbs to replenish energy stores.
Proper nutrition is personal and should be tailored to each child's needs, with education favored over dictation.
